newsitem.title: JAPAN: Impact of Japan sales tax rise lingering -- EPA.
newsitem.headline: Impact of Japan sales tax rise lingering -- EPA.

text.p: The impact on Japanese consumption of the increase in the national sales tax in April is still lingering, but consumption is likely to recover in time, Economic Planning Agency (EPA) Vice Minister Shimpei Nukaya told reporters on Friday.
The impact of the tax increase can especially be seen in June data for retail sales and car sales, he said.
"Looking ahead, however, we can see it (consumption) will recover in time, as has been clear in our surveys (of corporate and consumption trends)," he said.
The EPA has been saying that the impact of the tax increase will linger through the first half of fiscal 1997/98, but consumption will recover in the latter half, Nukaya said.
The tax's impact was strongest in the April-June period, he added.

"We must look at the figures before making judgments on how long the impact will linger after the April-June period, but there is a possibility that it might last to some extent into the July-September period," he said.

Nukaya said that he did not think the EPA's overall view on the economy differed from the Bank of Japan's (BOJ). There may be differing nuances in their views, however, deriving from how they assess different factors in the economy.

For example, the EPA would assess corporate capital spending as satisfactory, in an environment of slow economic recovery, as long as it grows enough to offset the fall-off in public works spending and prevents the economy from losing steam, he said.
The BOJ, on the other hand, may want to take a little bit more time to confirm that confidence has returned to smaller firms and non-manufacturers.
Nukaya said the BOJ may have expected slightly stronger capital spending than the latest data has shown.
"This point might be the slight difference between us," he said.
Japan's trade surplus is unlikely to continue the drastic expansion seen in the April-June period, Nukaya said.
"The surplus expanded too much, temporarily, in the April-to-June period," he said.

He did not explicitly say whether the surplus will continue to rise after June, but explained that the Japanese economy was basically expanding and that the impact of the trend toward a weaker yen was still continuing.
"The surplus will not rise, however, to a level where it would become a source of trade friction," he said.
